newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks off on election worries.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks off on election worries.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks dropped Wednesday following recent strong gains and amid a variety of worries, including the possibility that Democrats might regain control of Congress.

At 1 p.m. EDT, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 53.29 points at 6,008.51. The New York Stock Exchange's limits on programme trading were activated when the index lost 50 points in late morning.
In the broader market, declining issues swamped advances 2-1 on active volume of 245 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index was off 2.23 points at 1,217.77. The American Stock Exchange index was down 4.13 at 569.16.
"What we are seeing is a discounting process ahead of the election in November," said Joseph Barthel, chief investment strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
He said traders were considering the possibility of Democrats riding President Clinton's coattails to retake one or both houses of Congress.
Analysts said the market was happy with the present division of power and investors were jittery.

"Wall Street likes Clinton with a Republican Congress. A Democratic Congress could mean less curtailment of entitlements and less fiscal restraint, something the bond and stock markets do not like," Barthel said.
The six-year-old stock market rally picked up steam in November, 1994, after a Republican majority took over Congress. But mostly Republican Wall Street has grown accustomed to Clinton.
Analysts also said the market was overextended on the upside, and they questioned whether the corporate earnings momentum needed to keep it going could be sustained.

"We are up almost 13 percent in 65 trading days. Put a pencil to that and you can make the case that the market got full very quickly, and that calls for a normal consolidation," Barthel said. "I wouldn't rule out a visit to Dow 5,800."
In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury was off 5/32, and its yield rose to 6.87 percent from 6.86 percent on Tuesday.

Among the featured stocks, Conrail jumped 12-1/8 to 96-5/8, driven by Norfolk Southern Corp.'s $100 per share offer for the company, a bid intended to derail CSX Corp.'s friendly $92.50 per share merger pact.
Norfolk fell 7/8 to 93-5/8. CSX was off 1/4 at 46.

AT&T Corp. lost 2 at 37-7/8. The company named R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co. Chairman John Walter to the position of president and chief operating officer. Walter would replace Robert Allen as AT&T's chief executive in January 1998 and as chairman later that year.
Netscape Communications Corp. rose 2-5/8 to 47-1/8 after reporting quarterly earnings that exceeded analysts' expectations.
